newsitem.title: UK: Unequal health care biggest British issue - doctors.
newsitem.headline: Unequal health care biggest British issue - doctors.

text.p: British doctors attacked the state of the National Health Service on Friday, saying current policies would lead to a "shrunken NHS" and complaining that the election campaign did not offer any improvements.

Reports in the British Medical Journal said health targets would not be reached at current levels of funding, while a scathing editorial in the influential Lancet medical journal called the election campaign "passionless" and "frustrating".
"We believe that the first act of the new Secretary of State for Health should be to appoint a fresh working group on inequalities in health and the delivery of care," the Lancet editorial read.
"No UK political party has honestly addressed the matter of paying for the NHS," it said. "The financial crisis it is in and the one to come is easily understood."

The ruling Conservatives say their wide-ranging health reforms have improved the efficiency of the NHS, while the opposition Labour party charges that the changes have ruined a once-proud institution.
The Lancet complained that Britain spent less on health than other developed countries.

"The UK spends 5.9 percent of its gross domestic product (GDP) on the NHS (and a further one percent on private health care). The average proportion of GDP spent on health by countries in the Organisation of Economic Cooperation and Development is 10.4 percent."
Yet politicians offered little change in the run-up to the May 1 national election.

"The two main political parties have promised to increase the health budget by only 0.3 percent between 1997 and 2000, while the average annual increase since 1979 has been over three percent," it added.

"Either both parties are dissembling about their spending proposals or they are willing the see the NHS cede more of its role to the private sector while it becomes a fragile, minimum health service."
Reports in the British Medical Journal (BMJ) indicated widespread pessimism among doctors.

Dr Allyson Pollock of St George's Hospital Medical School and colleagues said allowing private companies to invest in NHS hospitals would cut bed numbers by 26 percent in England and 30 percent in Scotland in the next five years.

"Rather than being a tremendous opportunity for the modernisation of the NHS, the Private Finance Initiative is likely to lead to a shrunken NHS that will not be able to provide a comprehensive range of health services to all sections of the community," they wrote in the BMJ.
Researchers from the Centre for Health Studies at Durham University questioned 257 doctors and found most wanted to reduce rates of heart disease and strokes -- the biggest killers in Britain.
But only a quarter thought they could reach the government targets of a 40 percent reduction in their incidence in people over 65 by 2000.
The doctors said they were hampered by an excessive workload, unrealistic timescales and lack of funds.
